article.title: The Feedback Loop Problem: When Predictions Change the Data They Later Learn From
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Machine-learning systems do not always observe a passive world. Once predictions influence actions, those actions can change the data that future models receive. This creates a feedback loop between prediction, policy, observation, and retraining. Consider a fraud model. Transactions with high risk scores are sent for investigation, while low-risk transactions receive little scrutiny. Confirmed fraud labels will therefore be more complete among reviewed cases. When the next model is trained, it may learn from labels that were partly created by the previous model’s review policy. A marketing system has a similar problem. If only high-scoring customers receive offers, the organization observes treatment responses mainly in that selected population. Low-scoring customers provide little information about how they might have responded. Credit approval creates an even stronger form of selective labels: repayment outcomes are observed for approved applicants but not for rejected ones. Feedback loops can reinforce historical decisions. If a model sends more resources to one group, that group may generate more positive outcomes or more complete labels, which can make the next model favor it again. This does not mean every feedback loop is harmful. Recommendation systems intentionally learn from user reactions to previous recommendations. The problem is that observed data is endogenous to the policy: it reflects both underlying behavior and the system’s past actions. Analysts need to record treatment, eligibility, decision rules, model versions, and exposure. Randomized exploration can preserve information outside the current policy by assigning some actions independently of model scores. Holdout groups can measure what would happen without an intervention. In other settings, inverse-propensity weighting, doubly robust estimation, or other causal methods may help correct known selection processes, but they rely on assumptions and good logging. Monitoring should examine not only predictive performance but also changes in who receives actions and who receives labels. A model can appear stable while the observable population becomes progressively narrower. Retraining more frequently does not solve the problem if each new dataset inherits the same policy bias. Governance therefore needs a distinction between a prediction model and the data-collection policy surrounding it. Teams should ask whether every important region of the decision space continues to produce observable outcomes. They should also consider exploration costs: collecting counterfactual information may require deliberately taking actions that are not currently estimated to be optimal. The value of that information can be substantial when policies will be updated repeatedly. Feedback loops matter because machine learning changes the environment it measures. Historical data after deployment is not merely new evidence about customers; it is evidence generated under a particular model-driven policy. Recognizing that fact helps organizations avoid confusing the consequences of yesterday’s decisions with neutral facts about tomorrow’s population. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文強調分析結果必須放回正確的 baseline、母體、segment、decision cost 與資料生成機制中理解。百分比、總體 KPI、model threshold 或部署後的新資料，都可能因分母、selection、population mix 或舊 policy 而改變含義。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：分析結果はbaseline、母集団、segment、decision cost、data generating mechanismと結び付けて解釈する必要がある。percentage、集計KPI、model threshold、deployment後のdataは、分母、selection、population mix、過去policyによって意味が変わり得る。
